To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the trace element status of chicks was altered in a number of ways by the interaction of stress, E. coli, and EDTA.
the interaction of E. coli infection, stress, and dietary ethylenedianinetetraacide acid (EDTA) resulted in changes in serum and organ trace mineral levels in chicks.
the interaction of stress, E. coli infection, and dietary EDTA resulted in changes in tissue trace elements that were associated with increased susceptibility to E. coli infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of E. coli infection and stress on tissue trace element levels and organ weights in chicks.
the interaction of dietary EDTA and stress on E. coli infection in chicks.
the effect of E. coli infection, crowing stress, and dietary EDTA on trace elements and organ weights.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the trace element levels in the serum and organs of chicks were affected by stress, E. coli, EDTA, and the interactions between these factors.
the trace elements are affected by EDTA, stress and infection, but the effects are not consistent.
the effects of EDTA ingestion on trace element metabolism in chicks is complex and is influenced by the stress of E. coli infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
E. coli infection and EDTA ingestion interact to affect serum, hepatic and splenial Cu, Fe, Zn, and organ weights as a percentage to BW.
E. coli infection increased the mortality rate and decreased serum and bursa Fe in chicks that were stressed and fed a diet containing 0.1% EDTA.
E. coli infection and crowding stress interact to decrease serum Cu and Fe and increase serum Zn.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of EDTA on trace element status are complex and can interact in unexpected ways with other stressors.

trace elements in the serum and organs of chicks are affected by E. coli infection, stress, and EDT, and that these factors interact to produce a synergistic effect on the levels of trace elements in serum and tissues.
EDTA ingestion can predispose birds to a greater susceptibility to E. coli.
